name: SQL
description: SQL is the language of relational databases: query, combine, change and design data stored in tables.

blocks.html:
Databases & SQL Basics

What is a Database?

A database stores data in an organised way so it can be searched, updated and shared safely. A relational database keeps data in tables, like spreadsheets: each row is one record and each column is one property.

idnamecityage
1AyeshaLahore20
2BilalKarachi22

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language you use to talk to a relational database.

Kinds of SQL Commands

GroupPurposeExamples
DDL (definition)Create and change structureCREATE, ALTER, DROP
DML (manipulation)Change the dataINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
DQL (query)Read the dataSELECT
DCL / TCLPermissions and transactionsGRANT, COMMIT, ROLLBACK

The Practice Database

Every lesson uses the same small database: students, courses and enrollments (which student takes which course, with a grade). To follow along, paste this script into any SQL tool (for example SQLite, DB Browser, MySQL Workbench or an online SQL playground).

CREATE TABLE students (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  city TEXT,
  age INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE courses (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  credits INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id INTEGER,
  course_id INTEGER,
  grade INTEGER,
  FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES courses(id)
);

INSERT INTO students VALUES
  (1, 'Ayesha', 'Lahore', 20), (2, 'Bilal', 'Karachi', 22),
  (3, 'Hira', 'Lahore', 19),   (4, 'Zain', 'Islamabad', 21),
  (5, 'Sara', 'Karachi', 23),  (6, 'Omar', 'Multan', 24);
INSERT INTO courses VALUES
  (1, 'Databases', 3), (2, 'Web Engineering', 4), (3, 'Algorithms', 3);
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES
  (1, 1, 88), (1, 2, 92), (2, 1, 75), (3, 2, 81),
  (3, 3, 67), (4, 1, 59), (5, 2, 95), (5, 3, 84);

All outputs in this course come from a real run on SQLite. SQL is almost the same in MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server; the few differences are mentioned where they matter.

blocks.html:
• SELECT chooses the columns, * means all columns.
  • FROM says which table.
  • SQL keywords are not case sensitive, but writing them in UPPER CASE makes queries easier to read.
  • End a statement with a semicolon ;.

SELECT, WHERE & ORDER BY

Filtering with WHERE

WHERE keeps only the rows that match a condition. Text values go in single quotes.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, age FROM students WHERE city = 'Lahore';

SELECT name, city FROM students WHERE age > 20 AND city <> 'Karachi';
blocks.output:
name   | age
-------+----
Ayesha | 20
Hira   | 19
(2 rows)

name | city
-----+----------
Zain | Islamabad
Omar | Multan
(2 rows)

blocks.html:
OperatorMeaning
= <> < > <= >=Compare (<> means not equal)
AND OR NOTCombine conditions
IN (a, b)Matches any value in the list
BETWEEN a AND bInside a range (including both ends)
LIKEPattern: % = any text, _ = one character
IS NULLThe value is missing

Sorting, Limiting and DISTINCT

  • ORDER BY col sorts (add DESC for high to low).
  • LIMIT n returns only the first n rows (SQL Server uses TOP n).
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, age FROM students ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 3;

SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students ORDER BY city;
blocks.output:
name  | age
------+----
Omar  | 24
Sara  | 23
Bilal | 22
(3 rows)

city
---------
Islamabad
Karachi
Lahore
Multan
(4 rows)

blocks.html:
Column Aliases

Rename a result column with AS. You can also calculate in a query.

blocks.code: SELECT name AS student, age + 1 AS next_year_age FROM students WHERE id <= 2;

blocks.html:
INSERT, UPDATE & DELETE

INSERT

Add a new row by naming the columns and giving the values in the same order.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO students (id, name, city, age) VALUES (7, 'Noor', 'Quetta', 18);

SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 7;
blocks.output:
OK (1 row affected)

id | name | city   | age
---+------+--------+----
7  | Noor | Quetta | 18
(1 row)

blocks.html:
UPDATE

UPDATE changes existing rows. Always use WHERE: without it, every row is changed!

blocks.code:
UPDATE students SET city = 'Lahore', age = age + 1 WHERE id = 6;

SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 6;
blocks.output:
OK (1 row affected)

id | name | city   | age
---+------+--------+----
6  | Omar | Lahore | 25
(1 row)

blocks.html:
DELETE

DELETE removes rows. Like UPDATE, it needs a WHERE or it removes everything.

blocks.code:
DELETE FROM enrollments WHERE grade < 60;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS enrollments_left FROM enrollments;

blocks.html:
• Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows will be affected.
  • Use transactions (BEGIN ... COMMIT / ROLLBACK) to be able to undo a mistake.

Aggregates & GROUP BY

Aggregate Functions

An aggregate function turns many rows into one value.

FunctionResult
COUNT(*)Number of rows
SUM(col)Total
AVG(col)Average
MIN(col) / MAX(col)Smallest / biggest

blocks.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS students, MIN(age) AS youngest, MAX(age) AS oldest, ROUND(AVG(age), 1) AS average_age FROM students;

blocks.html:
GROUP BY

GROUP BY makes one group per value and applies the aggregate to each group.

blocks.code:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS students FROM students GROUP BY city ORDER BY students DESC, city;

SELECT course_id, ROUND(AVG(grade), 1) AS average_grade FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
blocks.output:
city      | students
----------+---------
Karachi   | 2
Lahore    | 2
Islamabad | 1
Multan    | 1
(4 rows)

course_id | average_grade
----------+--------------
1         | 74.0
2         | 89.3
3         | 75.5
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
HAVING vs WHERE

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after grouping (it can use aggregates).

blocks.code:
SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS enrolled, MAX(grade) AS top_grade
FROM enrollments
WHERE grade >= 60
GROUP BY course_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

blocks.html:
• Every column in SELECT must be either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
  • COUNT(col) ignores NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row.

Joins

Why Joins?

Good databases split data into several tables to avoid repeating it. A join puts the pieces back together by matching a foreign key in one table with the primary key of another. Here enrollments.student_id points to students.id.

INNER JOIN

INNER JOIN keeps only rows that have a match in both tables.

blocks.code:
SELECT s.name, e.course_id, e.grade
FROM students s
INNER JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE e.grade >= 90;
blocks.output:
name   | course_id | grade
-------+-----------+------
Ayesha | 2         | 92
Sara   | 2         | 95
(2 rows)

blocks.html:
LEFT JOIN

LEFT JOIN keeps all rows of the left table, filling NULL where nothing matches. It is how you find rows without a match, like students who take no course.

blocks.code:
SELECT s.name, e.course_id, e.grade
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE s.id IN (4, 6)
ORDER BY s.id;

SELECT s.name AS no_course
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE e.student_id IS NULL;
blocks.output:
name | course_id | grade
-----+-----------+------
Zain | 1         | 59
Omar | NULL      | NULL
(2 rows)

no_course
---------
Omar
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Joining Three Tables

Use table aliases (s, c, e) to keep queries short.

blocks.code:
SELECT s.name, c.title, e.grade
FROM enrollments e
JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id
JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
WHERE c.title = 'Databases'
ORDER BY e.grade DESC;
blocks.output:
name   | title     | grade
-------+-----------+------
Ayesha | Databases | 88
Bilal  | Databases | 75
Zain   | Databases | 59
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
JoinRows returned
INNEROnly matches
LEFTAll left rows + matches
RIGHTAll right rows + matches (not in SQLite)
FULLAll rows from both (not in MySQL or SQLite)

Subqueries

A Query Inside a Query

A subquery is a SELECT inside another statement, written in parentheses. The inner query runs first and gives its result to the outer one.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, age FROM students
WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM students);
blocks.output:
name  | age
------+----
Bilal | 22
Sara  | 23
Omar  | 24
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
IN and EXISTS

IN (subquery) checks against a list of values. EXISTS checks whether the subquery returns any row at all.

blocks.output:
name

(2 rows)

blocks.html:
• Many subqueries can also be written as a join. Joins are often faster and easier to read.
  • A subquery used where one value is expected must return exactly one row and one column.

Keys, Constraints & Design

Keys

KeyMeaning
Primary keyUniquely identifies each row. Never NULL, never repeated (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
Foreign keyA column that points to the primary key of another table, keeping relationships valid
Unique keyA column whose values must not repeat, such as an email

Constraints Protect Your Data

ConstraintRule
NOT NULLA value is required
UNIQUENo duplicates
CHECK (age >= 0)A custom rule
DEFAULT 0Value used when none is given
FOREIGN KEYMust match an existing parent row
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  age INTEGER CHECK (age >= 0),
  role TEXT DEFAULT 'student'
);

blocks.output:
Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: students.id

Error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

Error: NOT NULL constraint failed: students.name

blocks.html:
The database refuses bad data by itself, whatever the application does. (Error text differs between database systems.)

Relationships

TypeExampleHow
One to oneuser and profileA unique foreign key
One to manyone course, many enrollmentsForeign key on the "many" side
Many to manystudents and coursesA junction table (our enrollments)

Normalization in Brief

Normalization organises tables to avoid repeating data.

  • 1NF: each cell holds one value (no lists like "HTML, CSS" in one cell).
  • 2NF: every column depends on the whole key.
  • 3NF: columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. A student's city belongs in the students table, not copied into every enrollment row.

Indexes & Views

Indexes

An index is like the index at the back of a book: it lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of reading the whole table. Create indexes on columns you search or join on often.

CREATE INDEX idx_students_city ON students(city);
  • Indexes make SELECT faster but INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE slower, and they use space.
  • Primary keys and unique columns are indexed automatically.
  • Do not index every column. Index what you filter, join or sort by.

Views

A view is a saved query that behaves like a table. It hides complexity and lets you give users limited access.

OK (-1 rows affected)

blocks.html:
Transactions in One Minute

A transaction groups several statements so they all succeed or none do (think of moving money between two accounts).

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK; to undo both

This is the ACID idea: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
